stem:
What would be the average duration of year if the distance between the Sun and the Earth becomes
(A) thrice the present distance.
(B) twice the present distance.
The gravitational force between two bodies is 1 N. If distance between them is doubled, what will be the gravitational force between them?
solution:
Let the masses of the two bodies be \(m_{1}\) and \(m_{2}\) and the distance between them be \(r\).
The force between them, \(F_{1} = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}}\)
When the distance between them is doubled the force becomes, \(F_{2} = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{(2r)^{2}} = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{4r^{2}}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{F_{1}}{F_{2}} = \dfrac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}} \times \dfrac{4r^{2}}{Gm_{1}m_{2}}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{F_{1}}{F_{2}} = 4\)
\(\therefore F_{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}\) N \(\quad (\because F_{1} = 1\,\text{N})\)
\(F_{2} = 0.25\) N
\(\therefore\) Force become one forth (0.25 N)
_note: The book's closing line prints "one forth" for "one fourth". Transcribed verbatim; the numerical answer 0.25 N is correct.

stem: Three particles A, B, and C each having mass \(m\) are kept along a straight line with AB = BC = \(l\). A fourth particle D is kept on the perpendicular bisecter of AC at a distance \(l\) from B. Determine the gravitational force on D.
solution:
CD = AD = \(\sqrt{\text{AB}^{2} + \text{BD}^{2}} = \sqrt{2}\,l\)
Gravitational force on D = Vector sum of gravitational forces due to A, B and C.
Force due to A \(= \dfrac{Gmm}{(\text{AD})^{2}} = \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{2l^{2}}\). This will be along \(\overrightarrow{\text{DA}}\)
Force due to C \(= \dfrac{Gmm}{(\text{CD})^{2}} = \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{2l^{2}}\). This is along \(\overrightarrow{\text{DC}}\)
Force due to B \(= \dfrac{Gmm}{(\text{BD})^{2}} = \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{l^{2}}\). This is along \(\overrightarrow{\text{DB}}\)
We can resolve the forces along horizontal and vertical directions.
Let the unit vector along horizontal direction \(\overrightarrow{\text{AC}}\) be \(\hat{i}\) and along the vertical direction \(\overrightarrow{\text{BD}}\) be \(\hat{j}\)
Net horizontal force on D
\(= \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{2l^{2}}\cos 45^\circ(-\hat{i}) + \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{l^{2}}\cos 90^\circ(\hat{i}) + \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{2l^{2}}\cos 45^\circ(\hat{i})\)
\(= \dfrac{-Gm^{2}}{2\sqrt{2}l^{2}} + \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{2\sqrt{2}l^{2}} = 0\)
Net vertical force on D
\(= \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{2l^{2}}\cos 45^\circ(-\hat{j}) + \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{l^{2}}(-\hat{j}) + \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{2l^{2}}\cos 45^\circ(-\hat{j})\)
\(= \dfrac{-Gm^{2}}{l^{2}}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 1\right)(\hat{j})\)
\(= \dfrac{Gm^{2}}{l^{2}}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 1\right)(-\hat{j})\)
\((-\hat{j})\) shows that the net force is directed along DB
_note: The book spells "bisecter" for "bisector" in the stem; transcribed verbatim. The stem is self-contained (Fig. on p-05 illustrates the solution, not data the question withholds); the printed derivation is internally consistent and was re-verified.

stem:
Calculate mass of the Earth from given data,
Acceleration due to gravity \(g = 9.81\) m/s\(^{2}\)
Radius of the Earth \(R_{E} = 6.37 \times 10^{6}\) m
\(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\) N m\(^{2}\)/kg\(^{2}\)
Calculate the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of moon if mass of the moon is 1/80 times that of the Earth and diameter of the moon is 1/4 times that of the Earth (\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\))
solution:
\(M_{m}\) = Mass of the moon = \(M/80\), where \(M\) is mass of the Earth.
\(R_{m}\) = Radius of the moon = \(R/4\), where \(R\) is Radius of the Earth.
Acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Earth, \(g = GM/R^{2}\) --- (1)
Acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the moon, \(g_{m} = GM_{m}/R_{m}^{2}\) --- (2)
\(\therefore\) From equation (1) and (2)
\(\dfrac{g_{m}}{g} = \dfrac{M_{m}}{M} \times \left[\dfrac{R}{R_{m}}\right]^{2}\)
\(\dfrac{g_{m}}{g} = \dfrac{1}{80} \times \left[\dfrac{4}{1}\right]^{2}\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{g_{m}}{g} = \dfrac{1}{5}\)
\(\therefore g_{m} = \dfrac{g}{5} = \dfrac{9.8}{5}\)
\(\therefore g_{m} = 1.96\) m/s\(^{2}\)

stem: Find the acceleration due to gravity on a planet that is 10 times as massive as the Earth and with radius 20 times of the radius of the Earth (\(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\)).
solution:
Let mass of the planet be \(M_{p}\), radius of the Earth and that of the planet be \(R_{E}\) and \(R_{P}\) respectively. Let mass of the Earth be \(M_{E}\) and \(g_{p}\) be acceleration due to gravity on the planet.
\(M_{p} = 10\,M_{E}\)
\(R_{p} = 20\,R_{E}\), \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\)
\(g_{p} = ?\)
\(g = \dfrac{GM_{E}}{R_{E}^{2}}\), \(g_{p} = \dfrac{GM_{P}}{R_{P}^{2}}\)
\(\therefore g_{P} = \dfrac{G(10M_{E})}{(20R_{E})^{2}}\)
\(= \dfrac{10GM_{E}}{400R_{E}^{2}}\)
\(= \dfrac{1}{40}g\)
\(= 0.245\) m/s\(^{2}\)

stem: At what distance above the surface of Earth the acceleration due to gravity decreases by 10% of its value at the surface? (Radius of Earth = 6400 km). Assume the distance above the surface to be small compared to the radius of the Earth.
solution:
\(g_{h}\) = 90% of \(g\) (\(g\) decreases by 10% hence it becomes 90%)
or, \(\dfrac{g_{h}}{g} = \dfrac{90}{100} = 0.9\)
From Eq. (5.21)
\(g_{h} = g\left[1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\right]\)
\(\therefore \dfrac{g_{h}}{g} = 1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\)
\(\therefore 0.9 = 1 - \dfrac{2h}{R}\)
\(h = \dfrac{R}{20}\)
\(h = 320\) km

stem: Show that the critical velocity of a body revolving in a circular orbit very close to the surface of a planet of radius \(R\) and mean density \(\rho\) is \(2R\sqrt{\dfrac{G\pi\rho}{3}}\).
solution:
Since the body is revolving very close to the planet, \(h = 0\)
density \(\rho = \dfrac{M}{V} = \dfrac{M}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}}\)
\(\therefore M = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\rho\)
Critical Velocity
\(\mathrm{v}_{c} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{G\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\rho}{R}}\)
\(\therefore \mathrm{v}_{c} = 2R\sqrt{\dfrac{G\pi\rho}{3}}\)
_note: BOOK NUMBERING DEFECT: this example is printed "Example 5.9" on p-16 (printed page 94) and a DIFFERENT worked example is ALSO printed "Example 5.9" on p-18 (printed page 96). The chapter has 11 worked examples numbered 5.1-5.10 with 5.9 used twice and no 5.11. This one keeps the ref Solved Ex.5.9; the p-18 one is Solved Ex.5.9b. The derivation was independently re-verified and is correct.

stem: Calculate the period of revolution of a polar satellite orbiting close to the surface of the Earth. Given \(R = 6400\) km, \(g = 9.8\) m/s\(^{2}\).
solution:
\(h\) is negligible as satellite is close to the Earth surface.
\(\therefore R + h \approx R\)
\(g_{h} \approx g\)
\(R = 6400\) km \(= 6.4 \times 10^{6}\) m.
\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R}{g}}\)
\(= 2 \times 3.14\sqrt{\dfrac{6.4 \times 10^{6}}{9.8}}\)
\(= 5.075 \times 10^{3}\) second
\(= 85\) minute (approximately)
_note: Printed as "Example 5.9" on p-18 (printed page 96) — the SECOND example in this chapter to carry that number (see Solved Ex.5.9). Ref suffixed 'b' so the two do not collide; the book's own number is preserved in this note. Derivation re-verified: 2 x 3.14 x sqrt(6.4e6/9.8) = 5075 s = 84.6 min.

stem: An artificial satellite revolves around a planet in circular orbit close to its surface. Obtain the formula for period of the satellite in terms of density \(\rho\) and radius \(R\) of planet.
solution:
Period of satellite is given by,
\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(R+h)^{3}}{GM}}\) --- (1)
Here, the satellite revolves close to the surface of planet, hence \(h\) is negligible, hence \(R + h \simeq R\)
density \((\rho) = \dfrac{\text{mass}\,(M)}{\text{volume}\,(V)}\)
\(\therefore M = \rho V\) --- (2)
As planet is spherical in shape, volume of planet is given as
\(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\)
\(\therefore M = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\rho\) --- (3)
Substituting the values form eq. (2) and (3) in Eq. (1), we get
\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{R^{3}}{G \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\rho}}\)
\(\therefore T = \sqrt{\dfrac{3\pi}{G\rho}}\)
_note: The book prints "Substituting the values form eq." for "from eq." — transcribed verbatim. The result was re-verified independently and is correct.
